items.point: The Supreme Court has held that a person arrested for any offence, under any law including the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, must be given the grounds of arrest in writing, in a language they understand. If the officer cannot give them in writing at the time of arrest or soon after, the grounds must be told to the person orally. They must then be given in writing within a reasonable time, and at least two hours before the person is produced before the magistrate for remand. If this is not done, the arrest and the remand that follows are illegal and the person is free to go. The Court said this procedure governs arrests from its judgment of 6 November 2025 onwards.
items.law: Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra, Supreme Court (B.R. Gavai CJI and Augustine George Masih J.), 6 November 2025, Criminal Appeal No. 2195 of 2025, (2026) 1 SCC 500; paras 56 and 58 in the judgment's own numbering as printed and shown on Indian Kanoon (the conclusions are para 66 in the SCC report)
items.quote: 56. In conclusion, it is held that: i) The constitutional mandate of informing the arrestee the grounds of arrest is mandatory in all offences under all statutes including offences under IPC 1860 (now BNS 2023); ii) The grounds of arrest must be communicated in writing to the arrestee in the language he/she understands; iii) In case(s) where, the arresting officer/person is unable to communicate the grounds of arrest in writing on or soon after arrest, it be so done orally. The said grounds be communicated in writing within a reasonable time and in any case at least two hours prior to production of the arrestee for remand proceedings before the magistrate. iv) In case of non-compliance of the above, the arrest and subsequent remand would be rendered illegal and the person will be at liberty to be set free. ... 58. ... The ends of fairness and legal discipline therefore demand that this procedure as affirmed above shall govern arrests henceforth.
items.note: Read from the Indian Kanoon copy of the judgment (neutral citation 2025 INSC 1288 shown on it). The neutral citation is disputed, since Supreme Court Observer gives 2025 INSC 1295 for the same appeal and date, so the law line cites the appeal number and the SCC report only. The paragraph numbers are the judgment's own, which Indian Kanoon reproduces; the fact-check of 9 October 2026 records that the SCC report numbers the conclusions para 66 (not re-checked against the SCC volume). The (2026) 1 SCC 500 citation is taken from footnote 1 of Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab, Supreme Court, 21 September 2026 (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/144049703/). On whether it reaches earlier arrests: the judgment says 'henceforth' (para 58), and Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol, para 21.1.1, records that 'This Court in Sonam Raghuvanshi noted that the decision in Mihir Rajesh Shah is prospective. The same was rendered on 06.11.2025 whereas respondent-accused was arrested on 09.06.2025 much before the date of pronouncement'. Para 55 adds that if the remand is then sought, the application must explain the non-supply and the magistrate should decide it 'preferably within a week'. Jaskaran (para 21.1.2) also notes an observation in Sonam Raghuvanshi that release for non-service does not bar re-arrest; that is not in the point. Para 54 frames the rule as reading s.50 CrPC, now BNSS s.47.

items.point: No one accused of an offence can be forced to be a witness against themselves. A person the police question during an investigation must answer truthfully. The law excuses that person from answering questions whose answers would tend to expose them to a criminal charge, a penalty or forfeiture.
items.law: Constitution of India, Article 20(3); Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 180(1)-(2) (replaces CrPC section 161)
items.quote: Article 20(3): "No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself." BNSS section 180: "(1) Any police officer making an investigation under this Chapter ... may examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case. (2) Such person shall be bound to answer truly all questions relating to such case put to him by such officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture."
items.note: Article 20(3) from the Legislative Department's Constitution 'As on 1st May, 2026'; section 180 from the BNSS Gazette text (https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-04/250884_2_english_01042024.pdf). Article 20(3) protects a person 'accused of any offence'; section 180(2) covers anyone examined as 'acquainted with the facts'. The point therefore does not say a person may refuse to answer every question: section 180(2) obliges truthful answers except to self-incriminating ones. Nandini Satpathy (1978) is the usual authority applying Article 20(3) to police questioning; it was not opened for this entry.

items.point: Everyone must follow the lawful directions a police officer gives while carrying out duties under the chapter of the Sanhita on preventive action by the police. A police officer may detain or remove a person who resists, refuses, ignores or disregards such a direction. The officer may then take the person before a magistrate or, in petty cases, release the person as soon as possible within twenty-four hours.
items.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 172(1)-(2), in Chapter XII, 'Preventive action of the police'
items.quote: 172. (1) All persons shall be bound to conform to the lawful directions of a police officer given in fulfilment of any of his duty under this Chapter. (2) A police officer may detain or remove any person resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding to conform to any direction given by him under sub-section (1) and may either take such person before a Magistrate or, in petty cases, release him as soon as possible within a period of twenty-four hours.
items.note: Read from the Gazette text. The section does not say whether a record of the detention is made, and the point makes no claim either way. The twenty-four hour limit is stated only for release in petty cases; for taking the person before a Magistrate the section gives no time limit (Article 22(2) gives 24 hours if the detention is an arrest). 'This Chapter' is Chapter XII (sections 168 to 172), on preventive action, so the directions covered are those given in that duty. The Delhi Police Act, 1978, section 65 has a similar power in Delhi; it is not quoted here.

items.topic: 3. Force must be minimal and proportionate
items.point: The Supreme Court has said that police should use force only when it is absolutely necessary. When force is used, it should be the minimum needed and in proportion to the situation. It should stop as soon as the danger to life and property has passed.
items.law: Anita Thakur v. Govt. of J&K, Supreme Court (A.K. Sikri and R.K. Agrawal JJ.), 12 August 2016, Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 118 of 2007, para 12 (the judgment's own numbering, which Indian Kanoon shows)
items.quote: There are various documents in the form of police manual and even international covenants proscribing use of unnecessary force and mandating that force should only be used when it is absolutely necessary. Even when used, it should be minimum and proportional to the situation and its use to be discontinued as soon as the danger to life and property subsidised.
items.note: A footnote marker '2' after 'necessary' in the source is omitted; 'subsidised' is the source's spelling. The judgment has 16 paragraphs and Indian Kanoon reproduces its numbering; the fact-check records that later judgments cite this passage by the same para 12. The SCC citation was not shown on the page and is not given. The statute itself does not use 'minimum' or 'proportional' for the police: BNSS section 148(2) lets an Executive Magistrate or police officer disperse an assembly 'by force' with no stated limit, and the words 'as little force, and do as little injury to person and property, as may be consistent with dispersing the assembly' are in section 149(3), which binds officers of the armed forces called in by a Magistrate. The point therefore rests on the judgment alone. The same para also says police are 'required to undergo special training' for these situations.

items.topic: 8. Disobeying an order needs a public servant's complaint before a court can act
items.point: A court cannot take up an offence under sections 206 to 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, except section 209, unless the public servant concerned complains in writing. The complaint can also come from that public servant's superior, or from a public servant they have authorised. These sections include obstructing a public servant (section 221) and disobeying an order made by a public servant (section 223). The rule stops a court from taking cognizance of the offence. Its words do not stop the police from registering a case.
items.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 215(1)(a) (replaces CrPC section 195(1)(a))
items.quote: 215. (1) No Court shall take cognizance— (a) (i) of any offence punishable under sections 206 to 223 (both inclusive but excluding section 209) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; or (ii) of any abetment of, or attempt to commit, such offence; or (iii) of any criminal conspiracy to commit such offence, except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of some other public servant to whom he is administratively subordinate or of some other public servant who is authorised by the concerned public servant so to do;
items.note: Read from the Gazette text. The bar is on a Court taking cognizance; the section says nothing about registration of an FIR or investigation, and whether an FIR under these sections can be quashed for want of a complaint is argued case by case rather than settled. C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu (2010) 9 SCC 567, IK para 25, held a trial and conviction without the complaint void, while upholding convictions for other offences tried with it. Sections 132 and 195 BNS fall outside 206 to 223 and need no such complaint.

items.point: Voluntarily obstructing a public servant in carrying out public functions is punishable with up to three months in prison, a fine of up to 2,500 rupees, or both. The offence is non-cognizable and bailable. For this offence alone, the police cannot arrest without a warrant and cannot investigate without a magistrate's order. A case that also includes a cognizable offence is treated as a cognizable case as a whole.
items.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 221 (replaces IPC section 186); BNSS 2023, First Schedule, Part I, row for section 221, and Explanatory Note (2); BNSS section 174(2) and (4)
items.quote: BNS 221: "Whoever voluntarily obstructs any public servant in the discharge of his public functions, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both." BNSS First Schedule: "221 | Obstructing public servant in discharge of his public functions. | Imprisonment for 3 months, or fine of 2,500 rupees, or both. | Non-cognizable. | Bailable. | Any Magistrate." Explanatory Note (2): "the word "non-cognizable" stands for "a police officer shall not arrest without warrant"". BNSS 174: "(2) No police officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate having power to try such case or commit the case for trial. ... (4) Where a case relates to two or more offences of which at least one is cognizable, the case shall be deemed to be a cognizable case, notwithstanding that the other offences are non-cognizable."
items.note: Section 221 from the BNS Gazette text; the Schedule row, its Explanatory Note and section 174 from the BNSS Gazette text (https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-04/250884_2_english_01042024.pdf). Section 221 is obstruction. Disobeying an order of a public servant is section 223, already in the section on prohibitory orders, which the Schedule makes cognizable and bailable. Section 174(4) is why the point says 'for this offence alone': reports of the October 2026 Jantar Mantar FIRs say they also invoke section 132, which is cognizable, and if so the whole case is deemed cognizable. Section 221 is also within the section 215(1)(a) complaint bar. The Schedule row is printed in six columns that wrap across lines in the Gazette; the quote joins each column's text, with ' | ' between columns.

items.topic: 8. Obstructing police dispersing an assembly (s.195 BNS)
items.point: Assaulting or obstructing a public servant, or using criminal force on one, while the public servant is trying to disperse an unlawful assembly or put down a riot or affray, is punishable with up to three years in prison, a fine of at least 25,000 rupees, or both. The offence is cognizable and bailable.
items.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 195(1) (replaces IPC section 152); BNSS 2023, First Schedule, Part I, row for section 195(1)
items.quote: BNS 195: "(1) Whoever assaults or obstructs any public servant or uses criminal force on any public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant in endeavouring to disperse an unlawful assembly, or to suppress a riot or affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees, or with both." BNSS First Schedule: "195(1) | Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc. | Imprisonment for 3 years, or fine not less than 25,000 rupees, or both. | Cognizable. | Bailable. | Magistrate of the first class."
items.note: Section 195 from the BNS Gazette text; the Schedule row from the BNSS Gazette text (https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-04/250884_2_english_01042024.pdf). Section 195(2), threatening to assault or attempting to obstruct in the same situation, carries up to one year or fine or both and is non-cognizable and bailable. Section 195 lies outside sections 206 to 223, so the section 215(1)(a) complaint requirement does not apply to it. The IPC mapping (152) is from the usual correspondence tables and was not re-checked here. The Schedule row is printed in six columns that wrap across lines in the Gazette; the quote joins each column's text, with ' | ' between columns.

items.topic: 8. Assault or force to deter a public servant (s.132 BNS)
items.point: Assaulting or using criminal force on a public servant who is carrying out their duty, or to stop them doing it, or because of something they did lawfully in that duty, is punishable with up to two years in prison, a fine, or both. The offence is cognizable and non-bailable.
items.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 132 (replaces IPC section 353); BNSS 2023, First Schedule, Part I, row for section 132
items.quote: BNS 132: "Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person being a public servant in the execution of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person from discharging his duty as such public servant, or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by such person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both." BNSS First Schedule: "132 | Assault or use of criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty. | Imprisonment for 2 years, or fine, or both. | Cognizable. | Non-bailable. | Any Magistrate."
items.note: Section 132 from the BNS Gazette text; the Schedule row from the BNSS Gazette text (https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-04/250884_2_english_01042024.pdf). Non-bailable means bail is at the court's discretion (BNSS section 480), not that it cannot be given; that is not stated in the point. Section 132 lies outside sections 206 to 223, so the section 215(1)(a) complaint requirement does not apply. The Schedule row is printed in six columns that wrap across lines in the Gazette; the quote joins each column's text, with ' | ' between columns.

items.point: When the police apprehend a child alleged to have committed an offence, the child must be placed in the charge of the special juvenile police unit or the designated child welfare police officer. That officer must bring the child before the Juvenile Justice Board without delay, and within twenty-four hours of apprehending the child, leaving out the time needed for the journey. A child alleged to have committed an offence must never be placed in a police lockup or lodged in a jail.
items.law: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, section 10(1) and proviso
items.quote: 10. (1) As soon as a child alleged to be in conflict with law is apprehended by the police, such child shall be placed under the charge of the special juvenile police unit or the designated child welfare police officer, who shall produce the child before the Board without any loss of time but within a period of twenty-four hours of apprehending the child excluding the time necessary for the journey, from the place where such child was apprehended: Provided that in no case, a child alleged to be in conflict with law shall be placed in a police lockup or lodged in a jail.
items.note: Read from a scan of the Act as published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II, Section 1 (Gazette page 11), posted by Meghalaya's Social Welfare Department; India Code (indiacode.nic.in) and the CARA copy did not load from the sandbox. The text is the Act as enacted; the 2021 amendment is not believed to touch section 10, but this was not checked against a consolidated text. 'Child' in the Act means a person under eighteen (section 2(12)); that definition was not re-read for this entry, so the point does not state the age. Section 12 of the same Act deals with bail for such a child.

items.topic: 10. Complaining about force used by police
items.point: If the officer in charge of a police station refuses to record information about a cognizable offence, the person can send the substance of it in writing and by post to the Superintendent of Police. If that officer does not act on it, the person can apply to a magistrate, and the application must be supported by an affidavit. Where the complaint is against a public servant over something that arose in the course of official duties, the magistrate may order an investigation after receiving a report on the incident from that officer's superior. The magistrate must also consider the public servant's own account of what led to the incident.
items.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 173(4) (replaces CrPC section 154(3)); section 175(3) and 175(4) (replaces CrPC section 156(3))
items.quote: Section 173(4): "Any person aggrieved by a refusal on the part of an officer in charge of a police station to record the information referred to in sub-section (1), may send the substance of such information, in writing and by post, to the Superintendent of Police concerned who, if satisfied that such information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, shall either investigate the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by any police officer subordinate to him ... failing which such aggrieved person may make an application to the Magistrate." Section 175: "(3) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210 may, after considering the application supported by an affidavit made under sub-section (4) of section 173, and after making such inquiry as he thinks necessary and submission made in this regard by the police officer, order such an investigation as above-mentioned. (4) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210, may, upon receiving a complaint against a public servant arising in course of the discharge of his official duties, order investigation, subject to— (a) receiving a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior to him; and (b) after consideration of the assertions made by the public servant as to the situation that led to the incident so alleged."
items.note: Read from the Gazette text. Section 173(4) is about a refusal to record information of a cognizable offence; it is the step that section 175(3) refers back to. The statute names the 'Superintendent of Police'. In a police commissionerate such as Delhi the corresponding officer is usually a Deputy Commissioner of Police, but the BNSS text does not say so and the point does not name the Delhi officer; confirm the Delhi practice before adding it. Section 173(4) itself does not mention an affidavit; the affidavit requirement comes from section 175(3). Section 218 (sanction to prosecute a public servant) may separately apply at the stage of cognizance and is not covered here.
